pharm: Antidepressant (melatonergic) - EU/EMA approved, not FDA approved
quick: 25 mg orally once daily at bedtime; may increase to 50 mg after 2 weeks
Take at bedtime, with or without food
Limited data; use only if clearly needed
Avoid - excretion in milk unknown; discontinue nursing or drug
CONTRAINDICATED in hepatic impairment / transaminases >3x ULN
Liver function tests at baseline, 3, 6, 12, 24 weeks and on dose increase
summary: Agomelatine is a melatonergic antidepressant approved in the EU (EMA) for major depressive disorder; it is NOT FDA approved. It agonizes melatonin MT1/MT2 receptors and antagonizes serotonin 5-HT2C receptors, improving mood and resynchronizing disturbed circadian (sleep-wake) rhythms with a low incidence of sexual dysfunction and discontinuation symptoms. Its principal safety concern is dose-dependent HEPATOTOXICITY, mandating scheduled liver function monitoring; it is contraindicated in hepatic impairment.
indications: Treatment of major depressive episodes (major depressive disorder) in adults (EMA-approved indication)

dosage.d: Increase to 50 mg once daily if response inadequate
dosage.n: Repeat liver function tests before increasing dose

admin: Take once daily at bedtime, with or without food
Perform liver function tests at baseline and do not start if transaminases exceed 3x the upper limit of normal
Repeat liver function tests at approximately 3, 6, 12, and 24 weeks, and after each dose increase
Discontinue immediately if symptoms or signs of liver injury or transaminases >3x ULN occur
Continue treatment for an adequate period; no dose tapering is required on discontinuation
moa: Agomelatine is an agonist at melatonergic MT1 and MT2 receptors and an antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2C receptors. MT1/MT2 agonism resynchronizes circadian rhythms and restores normal sleep architecture, while 5-HT2C antagonism increases dopamine and noradrenaline release in the frontal cortex, producing antidepressant effects. It has no appreciable effect on monoamine reuptake and does not bind alpha/beta-adrenergic, histaminergic, cholinergic, or benzodiazepine receptors.

absolute: Hepatic impairment (cirrhosis or active liver disease)
Transaminases exceeding 3x the upper limit of normal
Concomitant potent CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g., fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin)
relative: Risk factors for hepatic injury (obesity, NAFLD, diabetes, alcohol use)
monitor: Liver function tests on the scheduled timetable
Suicidality, especially early in treatment and in young adults
Signs of hepatic injury (dark urine, jaundice, RUQ pain)

preg: There are limited data on use in pregnancy. As a precaution, avoid unless clearly necessary; weigh maternal benefit against potential fetal risk.
lact: It is unknown whether agomelatine or its metabolites are excreted in human milk; a risk to the breastfed infant cannot be excluded. A decision should be made to discontinue breastfeeding or the drug.
renal: There is limited experience in patients with severe renal impairment; use with caution. No specific dose adjustment is defined for mild-to-moderate impairment.
hepatic: CONTRAINDICATED in hepatic impairment and when transaminases exceed 3x ULN. Agomelatine can cause dose-dependent hepatotoxicity, including rare cases of hepatic failure - scheduled liver function monitoring is mandatory, and the drug must be stopped if liver injury develops.

major: Potent CYP1A2 inhibitors - fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin (markedly increase agomelatine exposure - contraindicated)
moderate: Moderate CYP1A2 inhibitors - propranolol, enoxacin, oral contraceptives (raise exposure - use caution)
minor: CYP1A2 inducers such as smoking (may reduce exposure)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.diagnostics: Can elevate serum transaminases (ALT/AST), occasionally markedly

serious: Hepatotoxicity (hepatitis, marked transaminase elevation, rare hepatic failure)
emergency: Acute hepatic injury / liver failure (jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain)

monitoring: Liver function tests at baseline, then at about 3, 6, 12, and 24 weeks and after any dose increase
Suicidal ideation, particularly in the first weeks and in patients under 25
Signs of hepatic injury (jaundice, dark urine, fatigue, abdominal pain)
counsel: Take one tablet at bedtime each day
Regular blood tests for the liver are essential - keep all appointments
Stop the medicine and contact your doctor if you notice yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, unusual tiredness, or stomach pain
Report worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm, especially early in treatment
pk: Antidepressant effect develops over 1-2 weeks; sleep benefits may appear earlier
Plasma peak within 1-2 hours of oral dosing
Once-daily bedtime dosing aligns with circadian action despite short half-life
Store below 30 C in the original packaging
pearls: EMA-approved (not FDA-approved) melatonergic antidepressant; this record is based on the EU SmPC/EPAR and BNF
KEY RISK: dose-dependent HEPATOTOXICITY - scheduled LFT monitoring is mandatory and it is contraindicated in hepatic impairment
Favorable profile for sleep (circadian resynchronization), low sexual dysfunction, and minimal discontinuation/withdrawal symptoms
Potent CYP1A2 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin) are contraindicated due to large rises in agomelatine exposure
missed: If a dose is missed, skip it and take the next dose at the usual bedtime - do not double up.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited; reported effects include epigastric pain, drowsiness, fatigue, agitation, anxiety, and paraesthesia. Management is symptomatic and supportive with monitoring; there is no specific antidote. Given hepatotoxic potential, assess liver function. Dialysis is unlikely to be helpful because of high protein binding.
